I run a lot of meetings, and the question I fear the least is the one I cannot answer. That surprises people, so let me explain. When I do not know something, I give three things instead of one. First, what I do know. Off the top of my head, it is around forty. Second, how sure I am. That is an educated guess, not a promise, and it cannot be more than fifty because of the size of the team. Third, a deadline. I will double-check with finance and get back to you by four. Three sentences, and the meeting moves on. What kills a meeting is not I do not know. It is I do not know, said alone, with nothing after it. The room does not need certainty from you. It needs a number to work with and a time when the real one arrives.

English carries certainty in three small words, and once you hear them you cannot stop noticing them. Must, might, and cannot. If I say the client must be annoyed, I am not guessing wildly. I have a reason: they have written twice this week. Must is the strong one. If I say the client might be annoyed, I genuinely do not know, and I am opening a door rather than closing it. And if I say the client cannot be annoyed, I am almost as sure as with must, only in the opposite direction. Here is why this matters at work. People do not mind when you are unsure. They mind when they cannot tell how unsure you are. Put the right word in front of your guess and you have told them everything they need. One more thing: after these words the verb never changes. It is must be, might be, cannot be. Never must to be.

First, I say what I do know, straight away: off the top of my head, it is around forty. Then I add the reason behind it, so the number is not floating in the air. After that, I mark how sure I am: it must be close to that, and it cannot be more than fifty. Next, I name the limit of what I know, so nobody treats my guess as a fact. In the end, I promise a real deadline: I will double-check and get back to you by four.
